statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether the vapour breathed out by people who vape harms the health of people nearby: no study read measured disease, or early markers of disease, in people exposed to it, so what is known is exposure. Compared with the same air before or without vaping, chamber, home and convention studies found higher airborne nicotine and fine particles than background in every study that measured them, by the National Academies' account (one home study's median fine-particle level matched a non-vaping home although it rose in real time during vaping; in a chamber with five people vaping, one-hour air nicotine 3.32 µg/m3 against undetectable and fine particles (PM2.5) 152 against 32.4 µg/m3; at a vaping convention an estimated 24-hour average PM10 of 1,800 µg/m3, 12 times the US 24-hour standard), rising with the number of people vaping; in homes, cotinine (a breakdown product of nicotine) in saliva and urine was higher in 5 non-smoking people living with someone who vaped than in people in control homes; and in six biomarker studies summarised by the UK review, short exposures produced no detectable change in nicotine, volatile organic compounds or tobacco-specific nitrosamines, while longer exposure during heavy sustained vaping raised nicotine or breakdown products of toxicants. Against second-hand cigarette smoke, levels were lower in the four studies that compared them (airborne nicotine 3.32 against 31.60 µg/m3 and PM2.5 152 against 819 µg/m3 in one chamber; 0.13 against 0.74 µg/m3 airborne nicotine in homes), which the National Academies rated moderate evidence while adding that the health effects of the lower exposures are unknown and that children, pregnant women, older people and people with heart or lung disease may be at special risk; a modelling study found a high-emitting device in a bar scenario exceeding acute reference levels for formaldehyde and acrolein, with estimated health loss in some scenarios comparable to second-hand smoke. A Dutch risk assessment (Visser et al., 2019) measured the first breath of 17 volunteers after one puff (nicotine in all but one, propylene glycol in 4, tobacco-specific nitrosamines in the 9 tested, glycerol in none) and modelled worst-case scenarios: the margins between modelled exposure and the level at which effects are expected were small for nicotine's effect on heart rate and blood pressure in a car (2.1), for propylene glycol irritation (17), and below the authors' threshold for nitrosamines and tumour risk in both a car and an office (521 and 2,297 against 10,000); nothing was measured in a room, a car or a person nearby, and the authors call the effects relatively mild even in the extreme scenario. The Australian review rated the rise in indoor particulate matter conclusive and airborne nicotine limited, and the evidence that these are at hazardous levels insufficient (Banks et al., 2023). The studies were single sessions of minutes to hours or one-off home measurements, in small groups, and mostly published between 2014 and 2017; no study followed people nearby for weeks or years. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated (the exposure findings).
plain: When someone vapes in a room, studies find more nicotine and tiny particles in the air than before, but less than cigarette smoke gives off. In the few homes tested, people living with someone who vaped had more of a nicotine breakdown product in saliva and urine than people in homes without vaping. Nobody has measured whether this harms the health of people nearby: no study read followed them for disease. A Dutch computer model of worst-case rooms found small safety margins for some chemicals, but nothing was measured in a real room, car or person. The studies were short, small and mostly from 2014 to 2017.
population: People who do not vape who are near someone vaping (volunteers in chambers and rooms, people living with someone who vapes, people at vaping conventions); 17 adults who vaped daily whose breath was measured (Netherlands)
exposure: Breathing air in which someone has vaped (second-hand vapour)
comparator: The same air without vaping (background), and, in four studies, air with cigarette smoke
outcome: Health effects in people nearby (not measured in any study read); exposure measures: airborne nicotine, fine particles and other chemicals, and nicotine biomarkers
magnitude: Health effects in people nearby: not measured in any study read. Exposure, as the National Academies describe the studies (vaping against baseline or control): chamber with 5 people vaping, one-hour air nicotine 3.32 (SD 2.49) vs undetectable µg/m3 and PM2.5 152 (86.8) vs 32.4 µg/m3; 9 volunteers for 2 hours in a café-like room, PM2.5 197 vs 6 µg/m3 and nicotine 2.2 vs below 0.04 µg/m3; 37 volunteers over 4 hours, nicotine 0.38 to 2.83 µg/m3 (several-fold below workplace limits); homes of people living with someone vaping more than 2 hours a day vs control homes, median air nicotine 0.11 vs 0.01 µg/m3, salivary cotinine 0.24 vs 0.05 ng/mL, urinary cotinine 2.64 vs 0.72 ng/mL; convention, estimated 24-hour PM10 1,800 µg/m3. Against second-hand cigarette smoke: one chamber, airborne nicotine 3.32 vs 31.60 µg/m3 and PM2.5 151.7 vs 819.3 µg/m3 (stated as 10 and 7 times; editors' calculation from the raw means 9.5 and 5.4 times); homes, airborne nicotine 0.13 vs 0.74 µg/m3 (5.7 times) and salivary cotinine 0.19 vs 0.38 ng/mL; surface nicotine 7.7 vs 1,303 µg/m2 (found in half of 8 vaping homes vs all 6 smoking homes). UK review: 6 biomarker studies, none from the UK; short exposures no detectable change. Dutch measurement and model (Visser et al., 2019): first breath after one puff, nicotine median 108 ng (below the limit to 2,140 ng), propylene glycol seen in 4 of 17, glycerol in none, nitrosamines up to 77 pg (NDMA equivalent); modelled car / office: nicotine 0.16 / 0.036 mg/m3, propylene glycol 9.5 / 2.16 mg/m3; margins 2.1 / 6 (nicotine, heart rate and blood pressure), 17 / 74–81 (propylene glycol, irritation), 521 / 2,297 (nitrosamines, against 10,000).

evidence.locator: Results › 3.3 Analysis of Exhaled Vapor, 3rd to 6th paragraphs; Table 3
evidence.extracted: In 17 adults who vaped daily (9 also smoked), using three tobacco-flavoured products chosen by the researchers and with their own breath before the first puff as the control, the first breath after one puff held nicotine in all but one person (median 108 ng, up to 2,140 ng), propylene glycol in 4 of 17 (up to 127 µg; median below the limit), glycerol in none (below the limit of quantification), tobacco-specific nitrosamines, measured in 9 people (total up to 77 pg as NDMA equivalent, median 28 pg, lowest value below the limit of quantification; no difference between people who also smoked and people who only vaped, p = 0.79), formaldehyde, acetaldehyde and acrolein in none of the 4 tested, and of 13 metals in 3 people only copper (up to 2.92 ng). Only the first exhalation after each puff was sampled.

evidence.locator: Results › 3.4 Bystander Exposure, 1st paragraph; Tables 4 and 5; Methods › 2.7, last paragraph
evidence.extracted: Modelled scenarios, not measurements in any person nearby: a car (2 people vaping at 0.5 puffs a minute for 1 hour in 2 m3 with no ventilation, the bystander a child; the authors say it approximates the highest exposure expected in everyday situations) and an office (1 person at 2 puffs a minute for 4 hours in 30 m3 with ventilation of 0.5 per hour; the authors consider it more indicative of typical exposure), both built from the single highest exhaled amount for each chemical and an assumed share of the inhaled amount (40% for local effects, 33% for systemic effects) appearing in the first exhalation. Modelled air concentrations (car / office): propylene glycol 9.5 / 2.16 mg/m3; nicotine 0.16 / 0.036 mg/m3; nitrosamines as NDMA equivalent 5.8 / 1.31 ng/m3; copper 219 / 50 ng/m3. Editors' calculation: the Table 5 values are reproduced from the Table 3 maxima and these settings.

evidence.locator: Results › 3.7 Propylene Glycol; 3.9 and 3.10 Nicotine; 3.11 Nitrosamines; 3.12 Copper; Table 6; Conclusions, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Margins between the modelled exposure and the level at which an effect is expected (car / office): nicotine's effect on heart rate and systolic blood pressure 2.1 / 6 (the authors say such effects should be expected in the car and cannot be excluded in the office, of a size they compare with the caffeine in 2 or 3 cups of coffee); propylene glycol airway and eye irritation 17 / 74 or 81 (cannot be excluded in the car, mild if it occurs); tobacco-specific nitrosamines and tumour risk 521 / 2,297 against the authors' threshold of 10,000 for low concern (risk cannot be excluded in the car and cannot be assessed with sufficient certainty in the office; all four nitrosamines were treated as equally potent as N-nitrosodimethylamine, which the authors say probably overestimates the risk). Local airway effects of nicotine were not expected in either scenario. Copper stayed below a tolerable air concentration.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Conclusions › Regulatory Implications; Abstract; Funding; Conflicts of Interest
evidence.extracted: The authors call the effects on bystanders relatively mild even in extreme scenarios, say the nitrosamine risk could be avoided if liquids had no detectable nitrosamines and that only a limited number of liquids on the market contain significant amounts (no citation in the passage), and describe this, to the best of their knowledge, as the first toxicological risk assessment of e-cigarette vapour to bystanders. The abstract states that vaping can clearly affect bystanders' health and names glycerol as an irritant, although glycerol was below the limit of quantification in all 17 volunteers. Funding as printed: Dutch Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport; the authors declare no conflict of interest.

Limits the authors state: only the first exhalation after each puff was sampled and the rest estimated with an assumed retention from a model developed for cigarette smoking; the highest concentration was used; the highest emissions seen probably do not represent the worst case with so few volunteers, and low-powered products probably lead to underestimation; changes of the vapour in air, nitrosamine formation from nicotine in air, and deposits on surfaces were not modelled; toxicity data are missing for most flavour compounds. Nothing was measured in a room, a car or a person nearby, and no cigarette was measured.

evidence.locator: Chapter 3 › Secondhand Exposure to E-Cigarette Aerosol › Characteristics and Chemical Composition of Secondhand E-Cigarette Aerosol, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: As described by the National Academies, in volunteers vaping in chambers and rooms: five people who also smoked, two 5-minute sessions of their own devices, one-hour air nicotine 3.32 (SD 2.49) µg/m3 against undetectable at baseline and PM2.5 152 (86.8) against 32.4 µg/m3 at baseline, no change in carbon monoxide (Czogała 2014); 37 volunteers over 4 hours with cigalike and tank devices, nicotine 0.38 to 2.83 µg/m3 with propylene glycol and glycerol up but several-fold below workplace limits, benzene, isoprene and toluene up (a 2017 chamber study); four volunteers, particles rising but lower than for tobacco smoke (Protano 2017); nine volunteers for 2 hours in a café-like room, PM2.5 197 against 6 µg/m3 in control periods, nicotine 2.2 against below 0.04 µg/m3, with aluminium and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons also higher than in control periods (Schober 2014).

evidence.locator: Chapter 3 › Secondhand Exposure to E-Cigarette Aerosol › Characteristics and Chemical Composition of Secondhand E-Cigarette Aerosol, 4th paragraph
evidence.extracted: As described by the National Academies, in real homes: one 60-minute sampling in a vaping household found small real-time rises in PM2.5 coinciding with vaping, but a median (9.88 µg/m3) similar to the non-vaping home (8.32; Fernández 2015); in a second home study, median air nicotine 0.11 against 0.01 µg/m3, salivary cotinine 0.24 against 0.05 ng/mL and urinary cotinine 2.64 against 0.72 ng/mL were higher in homes of people who lived with someone vaping more than 2 hours a day than in control homes (all p < 0.01; Ballbè 2014; chapter 18 gives the groups: 5 non-smoking people living with someone who vaped, 24 in control homes, 25 living with someone who smoked).

evidence.locator: Chapter 3 › Secondhand Exposure to E-Cigarette Aerosol › Characteristics and Chemical Composition of Secondhand E-Cigarette Aerosol, 5th and 6th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: As described by the National Academies, at two vaping conventions particulate matter was markedly elevated, reaching levels typical of bars and hookah venues; in one, PM2.5 was still higher the day after than the day before (Soule 2016); in the other, the estimated 24-hour average PM10 was 1,800 µg/m3, 12 times the US 24-hour standard of 150, total volatile organic compounds rose during a cloud competition, and a 7-hour air nicotine concentration of 125 µg/m3 was reported, which the committee compares with bars and nightclubs (Chen 2017).

evidence.locator: Chapter 3 › Secondhand Exposure to E-Cigarette Aerosol › Characteristics and Chemical Composition of Secondhand E-Cigarette Aerosol, 8th paragraph
evidence.extracted: As described by the National Academies, two modelling studies (Logue 2017, Rostami 2016); the passage gives results for Logue 2017 only. In a home scenario the contribution of second-hand vapour did not exceed California 8-hour reference exposure levels except with a high-emitting device (4.8 V; up to 12 µg/m3 formaldehyde and 2.6 µg/m3 acrolein); in a bar scenario, formaldehyde (mean 135 µg/m3) and acrolein (28 µg/m3) exceeded the acute 1-hour level for the highest-emitting device and voltage and exceeded 8-hour levels in several bars under less intense vaping. Health-loss estimates (disability-adjusted life years; also Logue 2017) for device and voltage combinations were lower than, but in some instances comparable to, those estimated for second-hand tobacco smoke. The committee identified no study of health effects or early biomarkers of disease from second-hand e-cigarette aerosol.

evidence.locator: Chapter 3 › Secondhand Exposure to E-Cigarette Aerosol › Synthesis, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: The National Academies' synthesis: all studies measuring particulate matter and nicotine (with nicotine liquids) found statistically significant increases over background, higher with more than one person vaping and extremely high at vaping conventions; two studies detected toluene and other volatile organic compounds. The committee reads this as indoor air pollution that is lower than from second-hand cigarette smoke but above the smoke-free level set out by the Surgeon General and the WHO tobacco convention; children, pregnant women, older people and people with heart or lung disease may be at special risk, and workers at conventions may be exposed substantially. It states that no available study evaluated health effects, clinical or early biomarkers of disease, of second-hand e-cigarette exposure.

evidence.locator: Chapter 3 › Secondhand Exposure to E-Cigarette Aerosol › Synthesis, Conclusions 3-1 and 3-2
evidence.extracted: The National Academies judged conclusive evidence that e-cigarette use increases airborne particulate matter and nicotine in indoor environments compared with background (supported by chamber experiments, real-setting experiments and observational studies in homes and convention centres; markedly lower than second-hand tobacco smoke in experiments with a single person vaping; rising markedly with the number of people vaping) and limited evidence that it increases nicotine and other constituents on indoor surfaces. These are the committee's judgments.

evidence.locator: Chapter 18 › Harm Reduction from Passive Exposure to E-Cigarette Aerosol Compared with Combustible Tobacco Cigarette Smoke Among Non-Users, 2nd to 5th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: As described by the National Academies, the four studies the committee drew on for exposure among non-smokers to emissions from e-cigarettes compared with cigarettes (two measured people, two measured air or surfaces): 15 people who had never smoked, in three 30-minute sessions, blood-count indexes unchanged after passive e-cigarette exposure and the antioxidant markers unchanged after any condition, while passive cigarette smoke raised white-cell, lymphocyte and granulocyte counts for at least an hour (Flouris 2012); 54 non-smokers at home, airborne nicotine (geometric mean) 0.13 µg/m3 in homes with someone vaping against 0.74 in homes with someone smoking (5.7 times) and salivary cotinine (geometric mean) 0.19 against 0.38 ng/mL (Ballbè 2014); a chamber (air measurements only), one-hour airborne nicotine 3.32 against 31.60 µg/m3 and PM2.5 151.7 against 819.3 µg/m3 for e-cigarettes against cigarettes, which the committee gives as 10 and 7 times (editors' calculation from the raw means: 9.5 and 5.4 times) (Czogała 2014); nicotine on household surfaces (wipe samples) detected in half of 8 vaping homes against all 6 smoking homes, averaging 7.7 against 1,303 µg/m2 in the homes where it was found (Bush and Goniewicz 2015).

evidence.locator: Chapter 18 › Evidence Review: Methods, last paragraph; Harm Reduction from Passive Exposure to E-Cigarette Aerosol Compared with Combustible Tobacco Cigarette Smoke Among Non-Users, 1st paragraph; Synthesis; Conclusion 18-5
evidence.extracted: The National Academies judged moderate evidence that second-hand exposure to nicotine and particulates is lower from e-cigarettes than from combustible cigarettes. The committee identified no study of intermediate or distal health outcomes of passive exposure to e-cigarette aerosol, no long-term study comparing health effects with second-hand smoke, states that the effects of the reduced exposures on health remain unknown, that even low levels of particulate matter may confer risk, and that children, pregnant women, older people and people with heart or lung disease may still be at special risk. This is the committee's judgment.

evidence.locator: Summary page › Chapter 7: Biomarkers of exposure › Main findings › Secondhand exposure, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Main findings page › 2.2 Biomarkers of toxicant exposure, 3rd bullet
evidence.extracted: The UK review's systematic review found six studies of second-hand exposure to vaping aerosol using a variety of biomarkers, none from the UK, with exposure varying greatly from people at home to people at an indoor vaping convention. Short exposures did not produce detectable changes in nicotine, volatile organic compounds or tobacco-specific nitrosamines; longer exposures during heavy sustained vaping were associated with significant increases in nicotine or in metabolites of potential toxicants. The main findings page states no significant increase in toxicant biomarkers after short-term second-hand exposure among people who do not smoke or vape.

evidence.locator: Summary page › Chapter 10: Respiratory diseases › Main findings › Respiratory tests and imaging, last paragraph; Chapter 11: Cardiovascular diseases › Main findings › Secondhand exposure, 1st paragraph; Comparisons with other reports, 6th paragraph
evidence.extracted: The UK review concluded there was insufficient evidence on whether acute second-hand vaping affects lung function; only 2 small studies at serious risk of bias included second-hand exposure for heart rate or blood pressure, so no conclusion could be drawn. It repeats the Committee on Toxicity's conclusion that vaping is associated with some emissions of nicotine into ambient air, so that pharmacological effects of nicotine in ambient air may occur in some individuals, and says its own two small studies of short-term second-hand exposure did not allow clear conclusions.
evidence.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)

evidence.locator: Results › Health outcomes, Box 3, row 'Environmental hazards with health implications (25)'
evidence.extracted: The Australian review rates conclusive evidence of increased airborne particulate matter in indoor environments with e-cigarette use, limited evidence of increased airborne nicotine and of nicotine and cotinine on indoor surfaces, insufficient evidence of increased air levels of carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, propylene glycol, volatile organic compounds and carbonyls, and, in the same row, insufficient evidence that the environmental hazards are of a level hazardous to human health. Authors' judgments; Box 2 counts 25 studies for environmental hazards.

risk_of_bias.note: Small, mostly single-session studies (4 to 37 volunteers in chambers; 5 people living with someone who vaped), read here through the National Academies' and the UK review's descriptions, which cannot be appraised from the summaries; the one primary source read in full (card sc_visser_2019, 17 volunteers and a model with worst-case assumptions) is rated high risk of bias on the editors' checklist.

inconsistency.note: The exposure findings point the same way; levels differ with setting and number of people vaping (one home study found a median similar to a control home despite real-time rises), which the sources explain by exposure conditions.

indirectness.note: The outcome of interest, health of people nearby, was not measured; air and cotinine measures and a model stand in for it. Chambers and conventions differ from everyday rooms, and the studies are mostly from 2014–2017, with the devices of that period.

imprecision.note: Small samples are counted under risk of bias.

grade.reasoning: Observational and laboratory exposure evidence starts low and is downgraded one level for risk of bias and one for indirectness, which reaches the floor of very low. Worded as insufficient evidence on health effects, which is what the sources support: the National Academies, the UK review and the Australian review all say that health effects of second-hand vapour have not been measured or cannot be concluded. The National Academies' conclusive rating concerns the rise in airborne particles and nicotine, not harm. Status replicated applies to that exposure finding, shown by independent studies in different settings.
